what: hir-ty's stand-in for the item store's facts keyed every item, the record's own body included, by the hash of its `PortableIds` bytes, and those bytes carry the content ID of each file named; `def_of` turned the decode error into `None` with `.ok()?`. A record of a body read in a database whose file was edited then failed as "it names item .., which this database does not have", which reads as a missing item or an unstable key and was neither: the real facts name the body itself as `Rel::Own`.
cost: the failure was handed over as a possible consequence of plain item keys in answers; finding the real reason took reading the test double, PortableIds, the frozen encoder's header and its content check
cause: the double ignored the `body` argument `BodyFacts::def_key` documents (the body itself is "self"), and it dropped the decoder's own message, which names the file and both content IDs
class: a test double that does not keep the contract of the trait it stands for, and an error turned into an absence (rule 3)
prevention: a double of `BodyFacts` shares the relative-key rule with the real one: one `own(body)` in hir-ty that both blaze-item-hash `keys::relative` and the double call; `def_of` returning `Result<Option<..>, String>` so a decode error cannot become "not here"
fix: the double names the body's own item by a fixed `OWN` key and reads it back as the body's item; its doc says another item is found again only where its file is the same text. `def_of`'s signature unchanged (a whole port across four implementors)
